Opening

LAUNCH · Humanities · Spring 2 · Week 4

Extreme weather and unequal risk

Learning goal

Investigate extreme-weather hazards and risk.

How can data help us understand hazard risk?

I can explain hazard causes, effects and management, analyse data, evaluate risk and produce an evidence-based case-study report.

40 minutes, with flexible pauses. Point, speak, draw, type or write. A fictional example is welcome.

Word and evidence bank

A Japan 11 March 2011

A magnitude 9.1 earthquake occurred off north-east Honshu, Japan. Sudden movement on the subduction boundary displaced the seafloor and produced a tsunami.

USGS event record, official20110311054624120_30

Limit: Magnitude measures the earthquake; it is not a direct count of people affected.

B Effects and responses

Shaking and coastal flooding damaged places and disrupted people’s lives. Earthquake-resistant design addresses shaking; warnings, evacuation routes and higher ground address tsunami exposure.

Authored explanation of the case and risk-management principles

Limit: A sea wall or warning cannot eliminate all risk. Do not judge people without considering access and warning time.

C Heat and unequal risk

On 19 July 2022 the Met Office recorded 40.3°C at Coningsby, 40.2°C at St James’s Park and 39.6°C at Topcliffe. Outdoor work increases exposure; difficulty accessing cool spaces can increase vulnerability. Shade and accessible cool spaces can reduce harm.

Met Office July 2022 report, station table; risk explanation authored for teaching

Limit: This explains risk factors, not a medical assessment of an individual.

D Reading a hazard feed

A USGS event row can include UTC time, place, magnitude and depth in kilometres. A short feed is a dated snapshot. It cannot predict the next earthquake.

USGS earthquake feed documentation

Limit: Small samples, reporting thresholds and later revisions affect patterns.

Teacher brief

Teacher notes and answers

Teacher card

Extreme weather and unequal risk / LAUNCH_S2_W04

Outcome: Investigate extreme-weather hazards and risk.

Evidence to retain: F: risk explanation and two exit questions.

Forty minute route

Arrival 4 min; starter 3; model 6; shared task 7; check 2; independent 12; review 3; exit 3. Pause time is flexible.

Preparation

Choose one independent route. Print the evidence and shared cards, required visual or data sheet, route worksheet and exit. The organiser is one separate A4 page. Keep answers with staff.

Use non-graphic maps and data. A bigger magnitude does not automatically mean greater harm; exposure and vulnerability matter.

Access and regulation

Pre-teach terminology and model evidence use. Chunk sources and data; provide an initial frame, then reduce it. Maintain normal access arrangements. Extend by weighing limitations, alternative explanations and evidence quality. Adults support access and evidence selection without supplying answers.

Offer a predictable start, private response and agreed pause. No cold calling or forced personal disclosure. Rejoin at one clearly named next step. Keep teen-appropriate examples and the same learning goal across response modes.

Use sensitive content warnings where relevant. Do not ask for family details or personal experiences.

Assessment

Use questioning and the exit response to decide the next step. Record the learner’s individual contribution and the access support used.

UAS: no approved unit code is supplied. Match the learner’s evidence to the centre-selected unit and exact criteria before submission. This pack makes no automatic award claim.

Model and answers

Read these pages before teaching. Hide the model during independent assessment.

Question: What was recorded at Coningsby on 19 July 2022?

Evidence: C Heat and unequal risk: On 19 July 2022 the Met Office recorded 40.3°C at Coningsby, 40.2°C at St James’s Park and 39.6°C at Topcliffe. Outdoor work increases exposure; difficulty accessing cool spaces can increase vulnerability. Shade and accessible cool spaces can reduce harm.

Think aloud: 40.3 degrees Celsius in the Met Office case-study report.

Check: Why can the same heatwave create unequal risk? People have different exposure, buildings, resources and access to cool spaces.

Arrival answers

1. Accessible routes and timely warnings that enable movement to higher ground.

2. Related to movement of Earth’s plates

3. 40.3 degrees Celsius in the Met Office case-study report.

4. People have different exposure, buildings, resources and access to cool spaces.

Shared activity reasoning

1. High air temperature — Hazard event. This is the weather condition.

2. Working outdoors — Exposure. A person is in the hot conditions.

3. No access to a cool space — Vulnerability. This can make avoiding harm more difficult.

Exit responses

What was recorded at Coningsby on 19 July 2022? 40.3 degrees Celsius in the Met Office case-study report.

Why can the same heatwave create unequal risk? People have different exposure, buildings, resources and access to cool spaces.

Teaching and evidence record

Supplied scheme of work teaching sequence: Interpret a weather-hazard map and case-study evidence. Distinguish the event from exposure and vulnerability; independently explain effects and evaluate a management response.

Look for

F: risk explanation and two exit questions.

Accept accurate equivalents, including speech or exact scribing. Check the concept and use of evidence rather than length or handwriting. Record access support separately from content prompting.

BUILD: a concrete example with a reason or demonstrated action. GROW: explain or compare with a relevant detail. LAUNCH: connect evidence and reasoning; use a limitation when the outcome requires it. Keep RE responses non-GCSE.

Media

Original captioned teaching model made for this pack. It demonstrates the supplied reasoning; it is not historical footage, survivor testimony or a documentary. The full transcript and factual source credits are included.

Use manual steps for a calm pace. The silent MP4 has visible captions and a matching text transcript. External archive media is optional and should be previewed before class.
